content.thinking:
I'm planning the module structure, deciding to use plain objects for static parts and joints only for moving pieces like lids, while working out how parts without joints attach to the required root joint.

To avoid parts accidentally snapping to the hinge joint's position, I'll always explicitly specify the bone for each part rather than relying on nearest-joint assignment, and build helper functions that default to the base bone. I'm sketching dimensions for the chest and treasure pile and settling on a League of Legends-inspired style with saturated gold tones, glowing hextech-style gems, and dark navy wood with gold trim.

For the coins, I'm planning to merge many cylinder geometries into a single part per paint color to keep things efficient, using BufferGeometryUtils to combine them while keeping consistent indexed attributes for position, normal, and UV.

Each coin needs an emblem on its top face, so I'll merge circle geometries slightly above the coin tops textured with a darker gold star, building proper transform matrices from quaternions to align each face circle's normal with its coin's orientation. Then I'm planning the overall pile structure—a hidden squashed-sphere mound underneath with coins scattered across its surface, each oriented to match the mound's local normal direction.

For the mound itself, I'm designing a height function that blends several overlapping ellipsoid "dunes," computing surface normals via finite differences, and building a displaced heightfield mesh from a plane grid so the mound tapers to flat ground at its edges.

Now I'm positioning the open treasure chest at the back center and planning to spill the coin pile forward and to the sides from its opening.

I need to make sure coin placement skips the chest's interior footprint, since that area should instead show a heap of gold spilling above the rim around y=0.30. The chest itself is a body box roughly 0.92 wide, 0.36 tall, 0.56 deep, with an open lid.

Building the walls as a hollow box with thin sides so the interior is visible, then filling it with a dome-shaped heap of gold coins near the top. For the wood, I'm defining a cel-shaded paint with grain texture and vertical plank lines, colored in deep indigo-purple tones.

Writing plank paint logic...

Now I'm figuring out the lid: a hinged barrel-shaped lid attached at the back top edge, computing the hinge joint position in chest coordinates, and planning to build the lid geometry in its closed pose before posing it open around 110 degrees using a joint rotation.

Actually -100° feels more natural, keeping the lid from tipping too far past vertical while still clearing the chest top. For the lid's shape itself, I'm working out an arched half-cylinder cross-section in the YZ plane, extruded along X, to give it that rounded chest-lid silhouette with a modest rise.

Finishing the arch outline with ten arc points and setting wood thickness to 0.95, then applying the plank paint pattern consistently with the body's grain lines. For the lid's interior, I'm considering a lighter inner liner panel that becomes visible only when the lid is opened.

Working through the velvet lining geometry — figuring out which face of the thin box ends up visible once the lid rotates open, since the normal direction flips from facing down to facing the viewer after the -100° rotation.

For the lining itself, I'm settling on a crimson box with a quilted diamond texture and gold stitch lines rather than trying to model actual quilting geometry. Then I'm shifting to the gold lid straps — arching outward slightly larger than the lid's curve to sit on top of it as a decorative band.

Next I want a lock hasp plate on the body's front with a keyhole and small glowing gem, and I'm considering whether to add a small gold tab where the lid's arched front edge meets the body.

For extra detail, I'm thinking of adding a glowing cyan gem in the lock and a teal glowing rune strip decal across the front plate between the straps, placed as thin plane decals just in front of the box surface.

Now I'm building the interior coin pile as a gold dome mound with a reusable height function so I can scatter coins across arbitrary surfaces, then designing treasure items starting with a crown resting on the pile—banded with seven spiked points, each tipped with a gem, and a large glowing jeweled centerpiece.

Defining crown geometry...

Still shaping band gems...

Now I'm planning the goblets: three tall gold goblets with gem studs, one tipped and spilling coins, each built from a lathe profile defining the foot, stem, and bowl curves.

I'm tracing the lathe profile from axis out to rim then back down inside with sharp creases preserved, using default segment counts. For variety, I'll make goblet variants in gold, silver, and bronze with matching gem colors, plus tipped-over versions spilling coin trails, and add faceted gem clusters using low-poly icosahedra for crystal formations.

For the brilliant-cut gem shape, I'm building a geometry helper that stacks a cylinder crown with a downward-pointing cone pavilion, considering how emissive glow at full brightness might wash out the facet shading since everything would read as the same flat color.

I think a glow strength around 0.55-0.6 keeps the facets visible while still brightening the gems, so I'll use that for larger gems and full strength 1.0 for small ones and runes. I'm also planning hex-prism crystal clusters with pointed cone tips, tilted and glowing magenta like amethyst, placed as a couple of clusters toward the back.

Beyond that, I want a big diamond gem displayed in front, plus scattered smaller gems merged by color (around 14 per color across 5 colors) using indexed cylinder+cone geometry so they merge cleanly with normals recomputed. I'm also adding a gold chain with a gem pendant draped across the pile using a Catmull-Rom sweep, along with a pearl strand made of merged white spheres.

Now I'm figuring out the pearls' placement along the path, evaluating the height at each point and offsetting upward slightly. I also want a gold ingot stack off to one side, built by extruding a trapezoid cross-section and arranging six bars in a pyramid (3-2-1), and I'm working out the exact dimensions for each ingot.

I'm setting the ingot proportions and extrusion thickness, tapering the top so it narrows, adding a small bevel, and giving each bar a darker stamped rectangle on top for detail. I'm placing the stack on a flatter region of the floor near the front-left to avoid conflicting with the mound heightfield, and planning "no-coin zones" so scattered coins don't overlap the ingots -- plus adding some coin stacks of eight scattered near the base.

Now I'm thinking through a spilling burlap sack of coins: lathe-generated bulgy profile with a crumpled top and rope-tied neck, tilted slightly, painted with tan burlap texture and patches, placed on a flatter region to the right where coins can tumble out convincingly. I'm also considering extras like gold rings with gems sitting on the pile, while deciding to skip swords, daggers, and treasure maps to keep the scene focused.

For grounding the whole composition, I'm adding a low octagonal stone dais beneath the pile for top-down readability, with a painted gold rune-ring using radial distance in the paint function, and establishing a floor offset so the dais top sits above the ground plane and the coin heightfield rests properly on top of it.

Now I'm checking overall scale — the dais at ~2.8m across feels right for the prop group — and working out the vertical stacking: chest base on the mound, hinge height, and lid rotation angle to get the full silhouette height when opened.

Setting the chest's position and hinge coordinates, then starting to lay out a list of surrounding dune shapes with their centers, radii, and heights to scatter around the chest base.

Tuning dune heights so the surface rises smoothly to meet the chest's front wall height, creating a continuous coin spill effect over the rim.

I'm defining exclusion zones so the chest footprint doesn't overlap the main coin scatter, then adding more pile mounds around the scene with varying heights and spreads for the side and back heaps.

Now I'm reworking the heightfield mesh extent so it doesn't poke out past the dais's circular edge—shrinking the grid and adjusting dune sizes so they taper to zero before reaching the disc boundary, avoiding any floating mesh corners beyond the dais radius.

Checking that the right dune extends within bounds, I'm defining the height function as a combination of dune bumps using a falloff formula—considering whether to use max (which creates creases) or a smoother sum instead.

I'll stick with max for simplicity since low-poly creases are acceptable, computing surface normals from finite differences of the height. For the coins, I'm estimating around 330 cylinders on the mound, each contributing roughly 48 triangles, putting the total polygon count near 16k.

For visual variety, I'm splitting coins into three color groups—gold, light gold, dark gold—using cel-shaded paints so the toon lighting creates distinct highlights and shadows on the rims and tops instead of flat uniform color.

I'm sizing coins small (0.05 radius, 0.012 thick) and tilting their orientation using an aim-direction quaternion instead of setFromUnitVectors, blending in randomness plus spin around the normal for natural scatter, while adding a star emblem detail on each face.

Since mixing one face texture across three coin colors causes a mismatch, I'll switch to transparent-background emblem textures with just the ring and star in darker gold line art, so transparent pixels get cut away and the coin's own color shows through underneath.

Checking stroke widths at raster size so the ring and star read clearly at small sizes, then settling on the emblem's outer ring, five-point star, and dot details in a muted brown-gold tone.

For gems, I'm organizing six colors—cyan, magenta, ruby, emerald, amber, and sapphire—to merge by hue group.

I'm building sixty gem meshes combining a short cylinder crown and an inverted cone base to form a faceted gem shape, sized small and merged for performance, with careful positioning so each gem's girdle sits correctly above the pile surface. For the glow pass, I need to make sure merged flat-colored gems are treated correctly versus painted materials to avoid breaking the shader logic.

Now I'm designing the interior gem heap inside the chest as a domed heightfield, computing a formula that raises the center and tapers toward the walls so the mound stays clear of the chest's inner edges, with the rectangular patch sized to match the chest's inner wall boundaries.

I'm planning to scatter around 90 coins over that interior field using the same height function, constraining their positions so they stay clear of the walls, and sketching out a generic scatter helper that generates positions and normals for each coin before cloning the geometry into bucketed arrays for efficient rendering. I'm also starting to think through how to build stacked coin groups along the vertical axis.

Next I'm figuring out how the mound surface should be shaded—computing smooth vertex normals on the heightfield grid and painting it a deep gold-brown cel tone to suggest coin coverage without needing sparkle detail. I'm also confirming how the `b.part` helper applies paints in model space using position and normal data, which should work cleanly for the heightfield geometry.

Setting up imports and a small local transform helper class to handle position/rotation composition for placing parts in local coordinate space, making sure every imported utility actually gets used to avoid lint errors.

Checking that sweep and joint calls accept bone references correctly—b.sweep takes a bone parameter fine, and joints are defined with parent/position/direction/role like the base joint with no direction and the lid joint set up as a hinge pointing along the z-axis.

For the coin geometry, I'm budgeting the triangle count: using low segment counts (around 10) per coin cylinder keeps each coin near 50 triangles, so even with 380-400 coins the total stays under 20k triangles, well within the 60k limit. I'm also checking that coin coverage on the pile mound (roughly 3 square meters of area) matches up with coin footprint, considering bumping the coin count to around 520 for better visual density with some overlap.

Now I need to figure out exclusion zones for coin placement—skipping areas where the chest or other larger items will sit—and make sure those items' base height is sampled from the mound surface function so they sink naturally into the coin pile rather than floating.

For individual item placement, I'm working out positions like the crown sitting atop a small dune near the front, tilted slightly and offset vertically to rest on the surface, with a footprint radius used to keep coins from overlapping its base too much.

Then I'm distributing the remaining treasure pieces around the dais: tall and silver goblets off to the left on their own dune, a tipped goblet further out, and the sack and ingots placed on the floor area, checking each against the dais radius so nothing falls outside the boundary.

Gem crystal clusters go into the back corners on the dunes, with large display diamonds up front sitting on their respective heights. I'm also scattering a couple of rings onto coin piles, with torus geometry for the rims and small gems set into them.

For the necklace, I'll build a pearl strand following a curved path across the dune using small spheres spaced along a catmull curve, plus a separate thin gold chain sweep with a gemstone pendant at the end. Then I'm moving on to the treasure chest details, starting with the wood plank coloring for the sides.

I'm settling on rich indigo-violet planks with high contrast against the gold, using a lit base color, a dark seam line, and cel-shaded shadows computed from the lit paint. I'm writing a function that paints alternating plank tones based on position, adds seam lines at plank boundaries, and layers in subtle wood grain texture on top.

For the lid's curved surfaces I'm orienting the plank direction consistently across x and z axes so the pattern reads coherently. I'm defining several cel-shaded gold variants for highlights and shadows, then estimating the total painted surface area across the chest, dais, and coin piles (roughly 18 square meters) to figure out the texel density needed for a 1024px atlas.

I'm bumping the paint resolution to 2048 for crisper cel-shading edges, deciding that's worth the extra cost over 1024. Now I'm working out the dais's painted texture, using polar coordinates (radius and angle) to carve out a ring of gold runes and dashed decorative bands into the stone surface, with the base color being a dark bluish-grey.

Since shadows are automatically computed from the light resolver, the gold ring will darken correctly in shadow while staying lit where surfaces face upward. I'm adding speckled stone texture by mixing between two greys using noise, and now I'm planning twelve glowing cyan rune nodes arranged in a ring around the dais, working out their exact radius so they sit near the gold band without overlapping it.

Adjusting the ring to r=1.33-1.40 with nodes at 1.365, keeping the dais radius at 1.45 and mound radius at 1.28 so dune extents stay within bounds. Now mapping the heightfield grid onto the disc and checking that the dune height values keep their x-extent inside the radius.

Checking the lid hinge area against the back dune rise — fine since it's hidden under the hinge. The chest body base and bottom trim are also likely hidden, so now I'm moving to check the chest walls themselves.

Defining the chest's floor, front, back, and side wall boxes with specific positions and dimensions, plus planning a dark crimson inner liner for the interior surfaces.

Adding gold trim as a slightly oversized box around the rim, positioned to stay hidden behind the interior walls while showing a thin outer lip at the top edge.

Now I'm placing the top rim frame pieces front, back, and sides as boxes, then adding corner posts and vertical straps across the front and back faces to simulate wrapped metal banding over the top edge.

Wait, a full-depth solid strap box would fill the chest's hollow interior, so I switch to thin front and back plates positioned just outside the wall surface instead of one continuous box through the body.

Now I'm adding gold rivet spheres at corner posts and strap positions, then designing a front lock plate with a dark keyhole cutout and a glowing gem accent on top, followed by gold filigree detailing on the front panel.

Between the straps, I'm placing two glowing rune decal planes in the empty spaces flanking the center lock, each showing a hexagonal cyan-stroked glyph drawn via SVG, sized and positioned to fit the available gaps on the front face.

Now I'm thinking through the lid construction, hinged at the back, with the lid's base plane sitting just above the rim top so it closes cleanly over the chest's opening.

Still plotting arc points...

I'm placing the hinge near the rim so the lid rotates open upward and back, and sizing the arch straps slightly larger than the base outline so they fit over it, making sure the strap bottoms extend down to meet the lid base properly.

Now I'm adding gold end caps to the arch at both sides, extruding thin semicircle plates with an expanded outline to cap the lid edges near the left and right extremes.

Then I'm placing a gold ridge rod running along the top of the arch between the two end points, plus a hasp tab box positioned at the front center near the base to serve as a lid latch detail.

I'll put the lock gem on the tab front glow and add a keyhole below on the lock plate. For the lid lining, I need to check placement carefully since the heap dome peak at y=0.48 exceeds the rim height of 0.44, meaning the lining position near y=0.43 could collide with the gold heap inside the chest.

Actually in the open pose this interior collision is moot, so I'll place the lining against the underside of the lid instead, visible from below when open, at y=yL-0.01 with 0.02 thickness so it doesn't poke through the lid surface.

Now I'm positioning rivets along the strap edges on the lid arch — four angular positions per strap, merged spheres along the arch surface for each of the two straps, plus accounting for the ridge rod.

All lid parts (lining, straps, rivets, ridge) need to be built in their closed-pose positions before I apply the pose rotation to the lid joint at the end, since anything built after the pose would land in the already-rotated frame. I'm also checking that the interior coin heap and scattered coins don't intersect the lid, and that glow elements on the lid move correctly with the pose.

Now I'm defining the crown's local geometry centered at its own origin, starting with a lathed outline for the band's outer shell profile.

Adding the band lathe profile...

I want the velvet to bulge above the crown band like a real hat, so I'm adjusting the dome scale to 0.7, giving a top height of 0.143 with spikes reaching up to 0.19, and tightening the dome radius to 0.112 to avoid clipping against the band.

For the spikes, I'm positioning eight points around a ring at radius 0.142, extruding a kite-shaped fleur outline along the tangential direction with a small notch near the tip, oriented radially using the tangent and up vectors at each angle.

I'm alternating tall and short spikes with different scales, and adding tip decorations—small glowing gems on the tall ones and plain white pearls on the short ones, offset slightly above the tip position.

For the band jewels, I'm placing them at the same angular positions as the spikes but at a fixed height, orienting each gem to point radially outward like a cabochon set into the band, with larger ruby-colored gems under the forward-facing spikes and smaller ones alternating between them.

I'm also adding a ring of tiny pearl spheres along the top rim of the band, and tilting the crown slightly on its base so one side sits lower, giving it a more natural leaning placement rather than sitting perfectly level.

Now I'm defining the goblet shape as a function that takes a transform, body paint, gem colour, optional liquid colour, and scale, building its profile as a series of points along the axis to form the bowl, stem, and base silhouette before revolving it into a solid form.

I check the disc radius against the inner wall at that height and it fits fine with glow strength 0.8. Then I consider adding a decorative gem ring at the stem node, deciding to use a small torus instead of individual gems...

Placing more decoration elements...

For the tipped goblet lying near the floor, I'm working out its rotation and position so the bowl rim and foot sit correctly against the ground, computing the center height from the bowl and foot radii.

I'll simplify and set the origin height, then scatter spilled coins in a short stream from the rim toward +x, flat on the dais floor with slight jitter and spin. Now I'm moving on to building the silver goblet with its own color variable.

For the three goblets, I'm giving each distinct materials and gem colors -- sapphire with magenta liquid, gold with ruby and emerald liquid, and a tipped bronze/gold variant -- then shifting to positioning the ingots as a rotated stack, working out the local x-offsets so three ingots fit side by side with small gaps between them.

Instead I'm restructuring the ingots into a tiered pyramid: three on the bottom layer spaced along z, two on the middle layer, and one on top, computing each layer's height and the tapered cross-section for an individual ingot so it tapers from a wider base to a narrower top edge.

I want to add a stamped emblem on top of each ingot using a flat box with a distinct color, vary each layer's gold shading slightly for depth, and introduce small per-ingot random rotation and position jitter so they don't look perfectly uniform. Now I'm turning to placing a sack prop near the dais, figuring out its position and radius so it fits within the dais bounds without overlapping other objects.

Still writing lathe profile points...

I'm also figuring out the sack's lean rotation and how the mouth opening shifts toward the lean direction, so I can place a coin spill heap on the ground near where the sack tips.

Checking the sack's position confirms it stays within the boundary radius. Now I'm adding burlap texture to the sack, a rope torus tied at the neck, plus short rope tails with a knot, and a sewn patch detail.

Then I'm thinking through decaling a coin emblem onto the sack's front surface—a gold coin with a star motif on a cream patch with stitched borders, positioned where the local coordinates approximate the visible front face.

Now I'm designing a crystal cluster generator: each crystal is a hexagonal shaft topped with a cone tip, merged into one part, randomly tilted outward from vertical, with twelve parts total across the cluster and a dark rock chunk forming the base.

I'm defining the specific cluster layout -- a central tall crystal with five smaller angled ones around it, colored magenta on the left and cyan on the right, plus some extra shards scattered nearby. Then I'm placing three decorative gems up front (a diamond, a ruby, and a crown-shaped gem), working out their positions and radii so they don't overlap.

Now I'm reorganizing the whole front area, laying out coordinates for a crown, a big diamond, gold and silver goblets on the dunes, a ruby and emerald, and a tipped goblet spilling coins toward the right, checking each item's radius against its neighbors to avoid collisions.

Still placing items... ingots, crystal clusters, rings, and a necklace chain whose path I'm plotting point by point to weave around the diamond and ruby without overlapping.

I'm also defining keepout circles around the crown, goblets, ingots, sack, gems, and crystal clusters so coins only scatter on the mound region rather than overlapping these larger items.

I'm sampling a smaller batch of coins directly on the dais floor beyond the mound, weighting acceptance toward areas with height above the floor while still allowing some bare-floor placements, keeping everything within the radius boundary so coins don't collide with the rune nodes.

I'm also considering adding floating star-sparkle cards above the pile, placing roughly a dozen small glowing quads at varying heights to give the treasure a shimmering, disconnected glow effect that fits the scene's style.

I'm also sketching interior coin placement for the chest handle area and thinking through how the coin face textures and SVG emblem decals should tint and layer so the darker brown emblem reads correctly against the metal.

Now I'm setting up the imports needed for the helper module, pulling in geometry merging, builder and frame utilities, math helpers for aiming and randomness, path curves for the necklace, and paint/texture utilities for grain, noise, and glow effects, making sure each import maps to a specific use like burlap grain, dais mixing, and sparkle framing.

I'm deciding to use smoothstep for gold flecks in the mound paint, blending two mound colors based on a noise threshold, and planning to use INK for keyhole and outline details. Then I'm drafting the metadata export with the piece's name, description, style, and commit hash, followed by defining a jewel-toned color palette and setting up cel-shaded paint definitions for the gold material.

Now I'm building a wood plank texture, alternating between two grain colors based on position along x or z depending on surface normal, with dark lines marking plank seams, then wrapping it in a cel-shaded paint...

Still defining more materials — burlap, rope, velvet crimson, and a quilted diamond-pattern SVG texture for the lid lining...

Drawing rune icon markup...

Computing star polygon coordinates...

Also sketching a 4-point diamond star shape with a soft glow center, then starting to draft a terrain heightfield builder function.

Verifying both triangle windings confirm consistent upward-facing normals, then setting up the disc-shaped UV mapping function with a square-root scaling for even radial distribution.

I'm building the BufferGeometry from positions and indices, computing vertex normals, and reasoning through whether paint baking needs UV coordinates—concluding the system likely defaults to [0,0] for parts without them.

For the dune height function, I'm defining a set of elliptical bumps and computing height as the max of each dune's parabolic falloff, then deriving surface normals via finite differences. I notice the square-root falloff creates vertical edges at the dune boundaries, making slopes too steep there, so I'm considering a gentler exponent or a purely parabolic falloff to smooth the transition.

Settling on using a sine-based easing for the dune height so slopes stay finite near the edges while still rising smoothly toward the center. I'm also checking whether the mound geometry under the chest pokes through the interior floor given the chest footprint and dune heights, and it looks like the center-back dune stays low enough to clear it.

That comes to about 0.427, close enough — the mound should stay hidden behind the wall exterior since walls extend to 0.44, but I'll lower the front dune height to 0.38 just to be safe. Now I'm redefining the interior heap function with the base level set so the rim sits at 0.44.

Checking the math again, the dome peaks around 0.49 at center with the heap base at 0.35 near the walls, leaving a 9cm exposed strip at the front before the ramp coins reach 0.44 at the rim — this looks like an acceptable overflow effect, not a full chest-overflowing look. I'll adjust so the heap base sits at 0.40 with the dome adding 0.12 to reach a peak of 0.52, keeping the base just under the rim height. Now I'm setting up the interior coordinate field for x and z ranges to match the chest's inner dimensions.

For the 85 interior coins, I'm writing a function that builds cylinder coin geometry plus a circular face overlay, positions them with a composed transform matrix, and sorts them into material bins, along with a helper for computing the tilt quaternion based on surface normal.

I'm also setting up keep-out zones around chests and other objects so coins don't spawn overlapping them, then writing a placement loop that samples random positions within the disc radius, rejects points in keep-out zones, and applies a sparser acceptance probability near the floor to avoid overcrowding.

With a target of around 470 coins and a cap of 6000 attempts, I'm positioning each coin slightly above the surface with small random offsets along the surface normal for a layered look, and giving coins a stronger tilt wobble on sloped terrain versus a gentle wobble on flat floor areas. I'm also checking that coins near the chest's front edge don't poke through the keep-out boundary given their radius.

I'm narrowing the chest keep-out region so coins stay clear of the front wall, trim plate, and corner posts, bounding interior placement within a rectangle that accounts for the gold trim and post thickness. For interior coins I'll compute height and surface normal using a numeric gradient of the floor function, and I'm now planning out several coin stacks at specific positions around the dais and near the spilled goblet, varying stack size and height.

Checking stack positions against the 1.25 radius limit and defining each coin's vertical offset, slight jitter, and a mostly-yaw rotation with a tiny tilt so stacked coins look naturally scattered, alternating colors between bins. For the spilled coin trail from the tipped goblet, I'm placing coins progressively outward along the goblet's rim direction with small jitter to simulate a scattered stream.

I'm defining a merged gem geometry combining a short cylinder and inverted cone to form a faceted gem shape, then scattering six gem colors with nine instances each across the mound surface, avoiding the chest and keep-out zones, with randomized outward-facing orientation and wobble, before merging each color group and applying a glossy flat-shaded material.

Now I'm setting up individual large gems with pose offsets sinking the apex into the surface, plus tilted ring parts using thin torus geometry oriented nearly vertical with small companion gems placed along their edge, building toward a function to position these ring-and-gem combos naturally on the pile.

Writing crystal cluster placement...

Now I'm designing the rock base using a flattened dodecahedron, scaled down vertically and stretched slightly for a squashed boulder look, with a mottled gray-violet color blend for a stone texture.

For the magenta crystal cluster, I'm planning two-tone coloring with a brighter tip against a magenta shaft, then layering in other glowing accents like a lock gem and the crown's front ruby for visual interest.

For the dais, I'm building a lathed decagon profile with a flat top and a stepped plinth edge, coloring it with the dais material tone.

Now I'm refining the dais profile points to add a second, wider ring step at the base for more visual depth, making sure the floor height stays consistent so the polygon closes properly against the axis and sits flush on the ground. For the top surface paint, I'm computing radius and angle to lay out a gold ring band flanked by dark ink borders, with plans for rune dash details further inward.

Then I'm adding sector-based tile lines radiating outward from the dais using angle divisions, checking that the line width stays thick enough to avoid aliasing at the texture resolution, and filling the rest with a noise-blended purple-blue base color. I settle on a default side/base tone, then move to placing twelve glowing cyan rune nodes along the structure.

I work out the rotation math needed to orient each box so its long axis aligns tangentially to the circle at its placement angle, deriving the correct rotation offset about the Y axis so the boxes curve naturally around the ring rather than pointing radially.

Now I'm adding gold hinge cylinders flanking the chest's back edge, sizing them small and positioning them at the seam between base and lid so they read as functional hinges while staying fixed to the base as the lid pivots.

I'm checking the lid's rotation math to make sure a -100° open angle swings it backward cleanly without clipping into the base, tracing how the local "up" vector transforms under that rotation to confirm the arc clears everything.

Lining normal faces +z after rotation, so the viewer sees the inside properly from a three-quarter front camera angle. I'm now working out the hinge rig and positioning the gem lock on the hasp relative to the lid's local coordinates.

The tab geometry sits along the lid's front edge so it rises when the lid opens, while the gem is placed slightly forward and up with its inward-pointing apex for the glow effect. On the body, I'm placing a static lock plate with a keyhole cylinder aligned along the z-axis plus a trapezoid slot cutout...

Now I'm working out rivet placement across the chest's corner posts and straps -- computing positions on the front/back and side faces of each of the 4 corner posts (24 rivets total) plus additional rivets along the front/back straps.

I'm deciding to skip adding hidden gold ball feet under the chest, but considering adding small gold ring handles on each end of the chest using a half-torus or arc sweep.

For the handle geometry, I'm working out a partial torus arc oriented in the YZ plane, positioned at the center height of each end face, rotating it properly so the arch hangs correctly on the chest ends.

For sparkles I'm scattering star-shaped cards at 14 positions, orienting each with a frame facing upward, and giving them a cross flow pattern with slight randomized variation before adding a glow pass over the meshes.

Writing transform helper class...

Still defining transform helpers...

Writing helper function...

Writing crown lathe transform...

Generating spike outline geometry...

Defining the extrusion points...

Still assigning radial gem colors...

Now adding a ring of merged pearl spheres at the rim using a geometry-merge helper, plus decorative torus rims for the band. I'm defining a goblet-building function that takes a transform, metal paint, gem color, liquid, and scale, starting with its profile curve of radius/height pairs.

Still writing goblet code...

I'll add a stem node torus and mirror the design for a silver goblet variant, sizing the gems around 0.011*s. For the sack, I'm adding a gold hemisphere peeking out from the mouth to suggest spilled coins, scaled and positioned to sit just inside the opening.

Then I'm scattering coins outward from the sack mouth in a fan pattern across the floor at varying distances and rotations, plus a handful tilted inside the mouth rim itself to sell the overflowing-treasure effect.

Now I'm working out the sack's placement and tilt, figuring out the Euler rotation order so the lean direction points toward the chest area it's resting against.

I'm placing the fanned coins along that same leaning direction, offsetting outward from the sack and sampling floor height so they rest naturally above the dune without overlapping the keep zone. Then I'm positioning the sack's emblem decal on its front face using a local offset and forward-facing direction vector.

Now I'm sketching the emblem SVG itself — a dashed-border circle with an inner ring, evoking a coin-like crest pattern for the sack's decoration.

I should keep the item positions pre-defined before any coin scattering happens, since their y-values come from H and don't depend on scatter order. I still need to work out the shared RNG for other details like mound painting, gem scatter, and floating dust glitter.

Now checking the tipped goblet's position and rotation—working through the Euler rotation math to figure out where its rim ends up relative to the coins, and I'm noticing the radius calculation for coins placed further out is exceeding the bounds I want, around 1.35 instead of staying within range.
